Apple has filed its opposition to OpenAI's motion to dismiss the lawsuit accusing two former employees, as well as OpenAI and io Products, of stealing its trade secrets. Here's the full story.

Background

A few days ago, OpenAI filed a motion to dismiss Apple's trade secret theft lawsuit against the company, io Products, Chang Liu, and Tang Tan.

In its motion, OpenAI argued that Apple filed the lawsuit "without adequate investigation" and laid out its own version of events.

OpenAI's opposition rests on three main arguments: that Apple "fails to identify protectable trade secrets," that Apple "fails to allege credible acts of misappropriation," and that Apple "fails to credibly allege any actual or ongoing harm."

OpenAI claimed that, contrary to Apple's allegations, former Apple employee Chang Liu was contacted by former colleagues after his departure, rather than accessing Apple data without authorization; while former Apple vice president Tang Tan retained Apple's offboarding documents to help ensure new employees complied with its security procedures.

OpenAI also argued that Apple's own information management and offboarding processes were to blame, claiming Apple encouraged employees to use personal iCloud accounts for work and failed to properly cut off departing employees' access to company data.

"Apple's complaint is about specific people, stealing specific secrets, in specific ways"

Today, Apple filed its response to OpenAI's motion to dismiss, systematically dismantling OpenAI's arguments and stating: "In short, Defendants do not grapple with the stunning core allegations in the complaint."

Apple argued that its original complaint "sufficiently identified the specific trade secrets allegedly misappropriated by Defendants," citing precedent that courts have found similar levels of detail sufficient to allow trade secret claims to proceed.

Apple also noted that OpenAI's argument that it failed to adequately protect its trade secrets is "equally unavailing," emphasizing that OpenAI "dismisses Apple's trade secrets as merely 'vendor relationships'—and then questions whether any 'vendor relationships' are secret at all."

In its opposition, Apple also directly responded to a heavily redacted conversation that OpenAI published on its website, involving a current Apple employee who proactively contacted Chang Liu to clarify information about an Apple project.

OpenAI argued that this conversation proves Apple's characterization of Liu's post-departure access as theft is misleading, since it was Apple's own employees who reached out to him for information.
